title: Imposition of Special Measure Regarding Huione Group, as a Foreign Financial Institution of Primary Money Laundering Concern
summary:
The U.S. Treasury’s financial crimes unit has finalized a rule that cuts off Huione Group, a Cambodia-based financial conglomerate, from access to U.S. banking through correspondent accounts. U.S. banks and other covered firms are now barred from opening or maintaining these accounts for Huione Group, and must add extra checks to make sure their foreign correspondent accounts aren’t used to process transactions involving the company. The rule takes effect November 17, 2025.

Why this matters: Treasury concluded that Huione Group is a primary money laundering concern. Investigators say the company and its affiliates moved funds tied to high‑profile crypto thefts linked to North Korean hackers and to large-scale online investment scams run by criminal networks in Southeast Asia. The group also promoted an “unfreezable” dollar‑pegged token, which regulators view as a magnet for criminals and an obstacle to recovering stolen funds. Officials also cited weak customer checks and efforts to obscure the company’s structure. Huione Pay PLC argued it is independent and is working on compliance; Treasury did not agree and kept it within scope.

Who benefits: Consumers and businesses targeted by online scams should see fewer avenues for criminals to cash out into dollars. U.S. banks get clearer guardrails, and law enforcement gains leverage by closing a channel that allegedly helped move stolen and scam proceeds. The move also supports national security goals by making it harder for sanctioned actors to raise and move money.

Who could be negatively affected: Huione Group and its affiliates will lose a path to dollar access, and any foreign banks tied to them may need to unwind relationships. Some legitimate users who relied on the company for payments could face disruption. U.S. financial firms will take on extra screening and notification tasks, though Treasury expects those costs to be modest because most already run similar controls.

Bottom line: This is a targeted step to keep suspected illicit funds out of the U.S. financial system, especially those linked to cyber thefts and online fraud. It signals tighter scrutiny of payment platforms and crypto services that market themselves as beyond the reach of regulators.
